transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-13
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Marina López (Redwood SE), Rajat Patel (Ironcladware - Head of AI), Maya Thompson (Ironcladware - Platform), Evan Chu (Ironcladware - FinOps)

Summary:
Rajat and team are evaluating Redwood for a production NLU feature but are under a tight monthly budget (~$5k–15k). Primary questions: hosted vs dedicated cost tradeoffs, batching and KV/prefix caching savings, commit/discounts, and security (SOC2/KMS/VPC). They want a pilot that proves unit economics and performance within a 6-week runway.

Topics covered: per-token pricing, batching impact, KV/prefix cache, dedicated reserved capacity and burst, private/VPC considerations, SOC2/KMS/audit logs, pilot scope and next steps.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we put the agenda in the chat. Quick round of intros, then dig into the budget constraints and the tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated and private.
[00:18] Rajat: Hey, yeah Rajat here. We're building an assistant that synthesizes compliance docs and it's pretty token heavy. Our finance folks handed us a tight monthly cap so cost is the gating concern.
[00:26] Maya: Maya, platform eng, I'll be doing the pilot run and integrating with our infra.
[00:31] Evan: Evan from FinOps — want to make sure we can forecast burn and have clear levers.
[00:36] Marina: Marina, Redwood SE — I'll handle the benchmark plan and walk through batching and caching levers.
[00:41] Alex: Cool. Quick clarifying q: ballpark monthly tokens you see?
[00:48] Rajat: Right now we're expecting roughly 8–12 million tokens/month in month one, potentially 20–30M in 3 months if adoption grows. But first phase target is under $15k/month.
[00:59] Alex: Ok that's helpful. Very much in the area where hosting is usually the fastest path but dedicated can make sense once you need predictability and lower unit cost.
[01:10] Evan: Can you give rough numbers? We need something we can stick in a forecast.
[01:15] Alex: Sure, rough directional examples — take a mid-sized decoder model: hosted per-token for interactive usage might be around low single-digit fractions of a cent per 1k tokens depending on model and context. With reserved dedicated capacity the amortized per-token can drop materially for steady throughput because you're not paying per-inference egress in the same way, but you need commit.
[01:34] Maya: Commit meaning monthly GPU reservation, right? How big a commit?
[01:38] Marina: Yes, reserved GPU pools. For example, a 1–2 GPU reserved pool for a smaller model, or larger for 8k/32k context models. The math depends on QPS and sequence length distribution.
[01:49] Rajat: Sequence length is pretty variable, average prompt+reply ~ 300 tokens but sometimes 4k when users paste long docs.
[01:58] Marina: That's an important point — long-tail sequences increase both cost and latency. We recommend a multi-tier strategy: shorter interactive queries served on hosted or smaller dedicated instances with high batching, and long-document requests routed to a higher-capacity node with appropriate SLOs.
[02:14] Evan: Ok, what's the impact of batching and caching? Can that get us under the $15k target for 8–12M tokens?
[02:22] Marina: Roughly, batching can reduce per-token compute by 20–60% depending on the batchability of your workload. KV/prefix caching can be massive if you have repeated system prompts or reused contexts; a 40–70% effective reduction in token compute on the cached portion is realistic for many document-heavy workflows.
[02:38] Alex: So if you see 30% effective cache hit + decent batching we can usually show a 2x improvement in unit-cost vs naive per-request pricing in the spreadsheet we'll send.
[02:48] Rajat: Those sound promising but we need concrete numbers in our cost model.
[02:52] Alex: Understood — we'll produce a per-scenario ROI table (hosted baseline, hosted with cache+batching, dedicated amortized with commit levels, private/VPC with ops overhead).
[03:02] Maya: Can you clarify private/VPC overhead? Our security folks prefer VPC.
[03:06] Marina: Private deployments have additional setup and ongoing ops costs — VPC peering, NAT, private control plane, and possible on-prem packaging if needed. Those show up as fixed monthly cost plus the same per-inference compute costs unless you self-host the runtime. We can estimate those as an overhead line item.
[03:22] Evan: What about discounts? If we commit 6–12 months, how does pricing change?
[03:26] Alex: Commit terms typically unlock meaningful discounts — it's a function of reserved GPU capacity and contract length. For many customers a 6–12 month modest commit (one or a few GPUs) reduces effective per-token by 20–40% vs month-to-month hosted rates in our examples. We'll model a few commit levels.
[03:41] Rajat: Our priority is predictability. If dedicated means we hit our SLO with a fixed monthly invoice that's attractive. But we also need burst for spikes.
[03:49] Marina: Dedicated can be configured with burst capacity for short spikes; you pay a smaller overage or burst buffer. Hosted is naturally bursty but less predictable on tail lat during platform-wide load.
[04:00] Alex: Another lever is quantization/precision: 8-bit or 4-bit quantized variants can cut GPU memory and throughput cost, but you need to validate quality. Marina can help run evals on your prompt set.
[04:10] Marina: Absolutely. For some models 4-bit works with minimal degradation for NLU, for others we recommend 8-bit. We'll include recommendation per-model in the benchmark.
[04:18] Maya: Security checklist — SOC2, SAML SSO, encryption, and audit logs. We're also mandated to use a customer-managed KMS for keys.
[04:26] Alex: Redwood supports SOC2, SAML/SSO, RBAC, and we can integrate with customer KMS for private deployments; for hosted we offer envelope encryption and a KMS integration plan. We'll share the security pack and network diagram after the call.
[04:40] Evan: Is there any difference in audit logs retention between hosted and private?
[04:44] Marina: Hosted has configurable retention tiers as an add-on; private gives you full control and easier integration with your SIEM. We'll note retention costs in the pricing sheet.
[04:54] Rajat: On the performance SLOs we want 95th percentile under 300ms for short queries, under 3s for long doc syntheses. Is that realistic?
[05:03] Marina: 95p under 300ms is aggressive but achievable for shorter sequences on dedicated or optimized hosted variants with KV caching and batching. Long doc synths will be higher; we can aim for 3s with the right provisioning. We'll capture latency targets in the pilot SLOs.
[05:17] Maya: We need to know how to instrument cost per route in the app — like charge a feature team internal showback.
[05:22] Alex: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and per-route breakout; you can tag requests and get a per-route dashboard. We'll demo that in the pilot.
[05:30] Evan: Ok great. For the pilot — what's a minimal pilot configuration that proves the unit economics?
[05:35] Marina: Minimal pilot: 4–6 weeks, run two routes: (1) interactive assistant short queries (300 token avg) routed to hosted/dedicated with batching & KV cache enabled; (2) long-document synth test (3–4k tokens) routed to dedicated larger node. We'll run load tests to project steady-state burn and show effective per-token cost with and without caching.
[05:52] Rajat: That key piece is the sample prompts — we'll share the three datasets.
[05:56] Maya: Yes we'll share both budget and compliance constraints in that dropbox link.
[06:02] Alex: Perfect; we'll take that and build the ROI model.
[06:06] [06:06] (short pause, typing)
[06:12] Evan: One more q — vendor lock-in risk. If we start on hosted and want to move to dedicated/private later, what's the migration path?
[06:20] Marina: The migration path is designed to be straightforward — same API surface and model versions. You can pin model versions and rollout policies in our control plane; dedicated/private uses the same endpoint abstraction so client changes are minimal. Biggest lift is data residency/networking for private.
[06:35] Alex: We'll show a migration checklist in the pilot scope doc.
[06:39] Rajat: About burst — how do we estimate overage charges if we get spikes from a marketing campaign?
[06:44] Marina: We can size a burst buffer and model overage at a premium rate in the ROI. We often recommend a reserved floor with a burst buffer that covers predictable spikes.
[06:54] Rajat: Sounds good. We also have some compliance customers requiring on-prem if we touch PII. Is on-prem an option?
[07:01] Marina: Yes, we have an on-prem package for air-gapped deployments; that has higher upfront engineering and licensing costs. We'll call that out separately.
[07:09] Maya: For the pilot, let's stick to hosted/dedicated hybrid — minimizes ops while proving costs.
[07:15] Alex: Works. We'll prepare cost scenarios for hybrid vs pure hosted vs dedicated.
[07:20] Evan: Can you show a worked example now? Even roughs help our finance model.
[07:24] Alex: Sure quick back-of-envelope: say average 400 tokens per request, 8 million tokens/month equals ~20k requests/month. If hosted baseline is X per token, and batching + caching reduces compute by 40%, that's effective saving of 40% on compute line. If dedicated with modest commit reduces per-token another 25% you can see cumulative improvements. We'll put numbers in the sheet — want that in 3 commit levels.
[07:45] Rajat: If you can show a baseline and two commit levels that'd help.
[07:50] Marina: We'll also include sensitivity to sequence length — because your 4k tail will change the math.
[07:55] Alex: On the pricing sheet we'll include per-token assumptions, per-GPU amortization, cache hit assumptions, and storage/retention line items.
[08:03] Maya: For the security docs you mentioned — when can we get them?
[08:06] Alex: I can send the security pack and the KMS integration doc today; full network diagram and SOC2 artifacts by EOD Tuesday.
[08:13] Evan: Great. Regarding pilot contract — what does Redwood typically expect? SLAs? Cancellation?
[08:18] Alex: For pilots we do a short MSA with pilot terms (no big commit), limited SLA, and a path to an enterprise contract if you decide to move to dedicated. We'll share a sample pilot MSA.
[08:29] Rajat: On metrics, we'll want cost per successful response and quality baselines (ROUGE/F1 or human rubric).
[08:36] Marina: We'll instrument both — automatic metrics + human evals for quality regressions. We can integrate your eval harness.
[08:44] Maya: Any gotchas we should watch for during the benchmark?
[08:47] Marina: Watch tokenization drift between model variants, and ensure your prompt canonicalization isn't inflating token counts. Also watch for cold-start KV cache misses during early runs — cache benefits increase over time.
[08:59] Evan: On the cost modeling side, please show worst-case and best-case for cache hit rates.
[09:03] Alex: Will do.
[09:05] [09:05] (brief cross-talk about calendar slots)
[09:12] Rajat: Are there any examples of customers in our space?
[09:15] Alex: We have a couple of regulated-document customers (we'll anonymize) that did a hybrid pilot and got 35% cost reduction after caching + batching tuning. We'll include an anonymized case study in the follow-up.
[09:30] Maya: Okay next steps recap?
[09:33] Alex: Recap: Redwood to send pricing sheet and security pack; Ironcladware to provide prompt sets and QPS targets; Redwood to schedule benchmark and draft pilot scope.
[09:43] Evan: I'll review the pricing spreadsheet with our FP&A and come back with questions — target to respond by 2026-08-19.
[09:52] Rajat: Good. If we can keep the pilot under $10k for the 6 weeks that'd be ideal.
[09:58] Marina: We'll model that scenario.
[10:02] Alex: Great — thanks all. We'll follow up with the artifacts.
[10:06] (meeting ends)

Notes / Links shared: Pricing spreadsheet (link in chat), Security pack (link), Benchmark harness repo: https://redwood.example/bench/ironclad-2026 (internal link).

End of transcript.
